title: Bladder Dysfunction: Urinary Incontinence and Neurogenic Bladder

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with three vaginal deliveries reports urine leakage when she laughs, coughs, or sneezes. Pelvic exam and urinalysis are normal. Which type of incontinence does she most likely have?
explanations: Incorrect. Urge incontinence presents with sudden urgency from detrusor overactivity, not leakage with cough.
Incorrect. Overflow incontinence presents with dribbling from retention, not stress maneuvers.
Correct. Leakage with cough/laugh/sneeze after vaginal deliveries reflects weakened pelvic floor and urethral support.
Incorrect. Functional incontinence is from mobility or cognitive barriers to reaching a toilet.
Incorrect. Neurogenic bladder requires a neurologic lesion; her exam is normal.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with longstanding BPH presents with continuous dribbling, weak stream, and nocturia. Post-void residual is 320 mL. Which type of incontinence is this?
explanations: Incorrect. Stress incontinence is leakage with increased abdominal pressure.
Correct. Chronic bladder outlet obstruction causes overdistension, with dribbling once pressure overcomes outlet resistance.
Incorrect. Urge incontinence is sudden urgency from detrusor overactivity.
Incorrect. Functional incontinence reflects access problems, not retention.
Incorrect. Mixed incontinence has features of both stress and urge, not retention.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has sudden, intense urges to void followed by leakage, with frequent small-volume urination and nocturia. Urinalysis is negative. Which mechanism best explains her symptoms?
explanations: Incorrect. Pelvic floor weakness causes stress incontinence, not urgency.
Incorrect. Detrusor underactivity causes overflow, not urge incontinence.
Incorrect. Outlet obstruction causes overflow symptoms.
Correct. Overactive bladder from detrusor hyperactivity drives sudden urgency and small-volume voids.
Incorrect. Sphincter denervation produces continuous leakage, not urgency.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on terazosin for BPH develops new leakage with coughing. Which mechanism best explains his worsening incontinence?
explanations: Incorrect. Alpha-1 blockers do not stimulate detrusor contraction.
Correct. Alpha-1 blockers relax the internal urethral sphincter, which can cause or worsen stress incontinence.
Incorrect. Alpha-1 blockers reduce, not worsen, outlet resistance.
Incorrect. Terazosin is not antimuscarinic.
Incorrect. Terazosin is not a diuretic.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis presents with urinary urgency and incontinence. MRI shows a cervical demyelinating lesion. Which bladder pattern is expected?
explanations: Incorrect. Flaccid bladder results from sacral or peripheral lesions, not suprasacral cord disease.
Correct. Suprasacral upper motor neuron lesions cause a spastic (overactive) bladder with urge incontinence.
Incorrect. Stress incontinence is a support problem, not from demyelination.
Incorrect. Peripheral neuropathy is not the mechanism in a cervical MS plaque.
Incorrect. MS spinal cord lesions typically disrupt the micturition reflex.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man sustains a T6 spinal cord injury in an MVA. After spinal shock resolves, which bladder dysfunction is most likely?
explanations: Incorrect. Flaccid bladder follows sacral/infrasacral lesions, not T6.
Incorrect. SCI above S2 disrupts coordinated voiding.
Correct. Suprasacral SCI preserves the sacral reflex but loses coordination, producing spastic bladder with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia.
Incorrect. Stress incontinence is not the SCI pattern.
Incorrect. SCI causes neurogenic, not functional, incontinence.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with severe lumbar disc herniation has urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, and decreased anal tone. Which neurogenic bladder pattern is most likely?
explanations: Incorrect. A spastic pattern requires intact sacral reflex arcs.
Correct. Cauda equina syndrome damages the S2-S4 sacral reflex, producing a flaccid bladder with overflow incontinence.
Incorrect. The micturition reflex is disrupted in cauda equina.
Incorrect. Stress incontinence is unrelated to cauda equina.
Incorrect. Dyssynergia occurs with suprasacral lesions, not cauda equina.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 20 years reports painless bladder distension, weak stream, and overflow leakage. Which mechanism best explains this?
choices: Bladder outlet obstruction from BPH alone
explanations: Incorrect. Diabetes does not typically cause CNS demyelination.
Incorrect. Stroke causes overactive bladder, not painless distension.
Correct. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy impairs sensation and detrusor contraction, producing a flaccid bladder with overflow.
Incorrect. BPH alone causes obstruction; painless distension implies sensory loss.
Incorrect. Detrusor hyperactivity causes urgency, not painless distension.

questions.stem: Which spinal cord lesion is most likely to produce a flaccid neurogenic bladder with overflow incontinence?
choices: Cervical spinal cord injury at C5
Multiple sclerosis plaque at T4 cord
Anterior disc herniation at L2 level
Hemorrhage in the pontine micturition center
explanations: Correct. The conus ends near L1-L2; posterior herniation at L2 compresses sacral nerve roots and disrupts the micturition reflex.
Incorrect. C5 injury produces a suprasacral spastic bladder.
Incorrect. T4 MS plaque is suprasacral, producing a spastic bladder.
Incorrect. Anterior disc herniation is less likely to compress the cauda equina.
Incorrect. Pontine lesions disrupt voluntary control but spare the sacral reflex.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man recovering from a left MCA stroke now has frequent small-volume urination with urgency. Which mechanism best explains his urinary symptoms?
explanations: Incorrect. Stroke spares the sacral reflex arc.
Incorrect. Stroke affects the CNS, not peripheral nerves.
Correct. Brain injury removes cortical inhibition of the spinal micturition reflex, producing an overactive bladder.
Incorrect. Pelvic floor weakness causes stress incontinence, not urgency from stroke.
Incorrect. Stroke does not cause outlet obstruction.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with overactive bladder is started on oxybutynin. What is its primary mechanism of action in the bladder?
explanations: Incorrect. Mirabegron is the beta-3 agonist; oxybutynin is antimuscarinic.
Correct. Oxybutynin blocks M3 receptors on the detrusor, reducing involuntary contractions and increasing bladder capacity.
Incorrect. Alpha-1 blockers target the prostate and bladder neck, not the detrusor.
Incorrect. Bethanechol is the muscarinic agonist; oxybutynin is the antagonist.
Incorrect. Oxybutynin acts via receptor blockade, not direct relaxation.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with urge incontinence is started on tolterodine. Two weeks later he reports dry mouth, constipation, and difficulty voiding with a new post-void residual of 250 mL. What is the best next step?
explanations: Incorrect. Higher antimuscarinic doses worsen retention and side effects.
Incorrect. Bethanechol is for hypotonic bladders; combining is not first-line here.
Correct. Mirabegron, a beta-3 agonist, treats overactive bladder without antimuscarinic effects and is preferred when those limit therapy.
Incorrect. Tamsulosin treats BPH outlet obstruction, not detrusor overactivity.
Incorrect. Diuretics worsen incontinence.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man started on mirabegron for overactive bladder returns with elevated blood pressure readings. Which property of mirabegron best explains this finding?
explanations: Incorrect. Mirabegron is not antimuscarinic.
Correct. Beta-3 stimulation can raise blood pressure; this is the key safety concern with mirabegron.
Incorrect. Mirabegron acts on beta-3, not alpha-1, receptors.
Incorrect. Aldosterone activation is not its mechanism.
Incorrect. Sodium retention is not the described effect.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has a hypotonic neurogenic bladder with urinary retention after pelvic surgery. Which medication directly stimulates detrusor contraction?
explanations: Incorrect. Oxybutynin blocks M3 receptors and worsens retention.
Incorrect. Tamsulosin relaxes the bladder neck but does not stimulate detrusor contraction.
Incorrect. Mirabegron relaxes the detrusor.
Correct. Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist that stimulates M3 receptors to promote detrusor contraction and emptying.
Incorrect. Solifenacin is antimuscarinic and worsens retention.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with BPH-related hesitancy, weak stream, and post-void dribbling is started on tamsulosin. What is its mechanism of action?
choices: M3 blockade on the detrusor muscle
explanations: Incorrect. Antimuscarinics target the detrusor; tamsulosin does not.
Incorrect. Mirabegron is the beta-3 agonist.
Correct. Tamsulosin blocks alpha-1 receptors on prostate and bladder neck smooth muscle, reducing outlet resistance.
Incorrect. Finasteride is the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor.
Incorrect. Bethanechol is the muscarinic agonist.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man takes doxazosin for BPH. After his first dose he stands and feels dizzy with near-syncope. Which adverse effect best explains this?
explanations: Incorrect. Bronchospasm is associated with bethanechol, not alpha-1 blockers.
Incorrect. Doxazosin is not antimuscarinic.
Correct. Alpha-1 blockers cause orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, and syncope due to vascular smooth muscle relaxation.
Incorrect. Doxazosin does not cause serotonin syndrome.
Incorrect. Hyperkalemia is not a typical doxazosin effect.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD and heart block needs treatment for a hypotonic bladder. Which medication should be used with greatest caution?
explanations: Correct. Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist that can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia, dangerous in reactive airway and conduction disease.
Incorrect. Oxybutynin does not cause bronchospasm or bradycardia.
Incorrect. Mirabegron raises BP but does not cause bronchospasm.
Incorrect. Tamsulosin is unrelated to these risks.
Incorrect. Solifenacin is antimuscarinic and would not worsen these conditions.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman has urgency, frequency, vaginal dryness, and mild incontinence. Pelvic exam shows atrophic vaginal mucosa. Which treatment best addresses the underlying tissue change?
explanations: Incorrect. Systemic estrogen carries higher risk; topical is preferred for GU symptoms.
Correct. Topical vaginal estrogen restores urogenital epithelium and improves urethral coaptation in GSM.
Incorrect. Tamsulosin treats male BPH, not GSM.
Incorrect. Diuretics worsen incontinence.
Incorrect. Bethanechol is for hypotonic bladder, not GSM.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with mild stress incontinence after vaginal deliveries wants nonpharmacologic management. Which first-line intervention is most appropriate?
explanations: Incorrect. Catheters are not first-line and carry UTI risk.
Correct. Pelvic floor exercises strengthen the levator ani and external sphincter, first-line for stress incontinence.
Incorrect. Suprapubic catheters are reserved for chronic refractory incontinence.
Incorrect. Neuromodulation is for refractory urge incontinence.
Incorrect. Augmentation surgery is not first-line.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with stress incontinence declines surgery. Which device is most appropriate to physically support the urethra and bladder neck?
explanations: Incorrect. Condom catheters are male external collection devices.
Incorrect. Foley catheters drain but do not support pelvic anatomy.
Correct. A pessary is inserted vaginally to provide muscular support and reduce stress incontinence.
Incorrect. Suprapubic catheters drain the bladder, they do not provide support.
Incorrect. Intermittent catheters drain but do not provide pelvic support.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a T8 spinal cord injury requires bladder drainage. Which approach has the lowest infection risk for long-term management?
explanations: Incorrect. Indwelling catheters carry higher UTI and epididymitis risk.
Correct. Intermittent catheterization is safer than indwelling Foley for chronic neurogenic bladder management.
Incorrect. Suprapubic catheters are reserved for chronic cases when other methods fail.
Incorrect. Continuous irrigation is not standard for neurogenic bladder.
Incorrect. SCI patients with retention require drainage.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with suspected incontinence reports frequency, hesitancy, and incomplete voiding. Which initial test is most important to rule out a treatable cause?
explanations: Incorrect. Urodynamics is a specialized later test, not first-line.
Incorrect. Cystoscopy is invasive and not first-line.
Correct. Urinalysis (with culture if needed) rules out UTI, a common reversible cause of urgency and incontinence.
Incorrect. MRI is not the initial workup for incontinence.
Incorrect. Renal ultrasound does not diagnose UTI or incontinence type.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with suspected overflow incontinence needs noninvasive assessment of post-void residual volume. Which method is most appropriate?
explanations: Incorrect. CT involves radiation and is not the standard method.
Correct. Bladder ultrasound estimates post-void residual without catheterization.
Incorrect. MRI is not the standard method for PVR measurement.
Incorrect. X-ray does not quantify bladder volume.
Incorrect. BUN/creatinine assesses renal function, not bladder volume.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has predominant urge incontinence refractory to behavioral therapy, oxybutynin, and mirabegron. Which procedural option is most appropriate?
explanations: Incorrect. Slings treat stress incontinence.
Incorrect. Artificial sphincters address sphincter weakness, not urge.
Incorrect. Bulking treats stress incontinence.
Correct. Botulinum toxin injection (or sacral neuromodulation) treats refractory urge incontinence by increasing bladder capacity.
Incorrect. Pessaries support stress incontinence, not urge.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with stress incontinence has failed pelvic floor therapy. Which surgical option is most appropriate?
explanations: Incorrect. Neuromodulation treats urge, not stress, incontinence.
Incorrect. Botulinum toxin treats detrusor overactivity, not sphincter weakness.
Correct. Midurethral sling procedures increase urethral support and outlet resistance, treating stress incontinence.
Incorrect. Augmentation increases bladder capacity for urge incontinence.
Incorrect. Suprapubic catheter is not a surgical correction for stress incontinence.
